math_p1_01.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(1)] (4 marks)

(a) Simplify $\dfrac{(2a^{3}b^{-2})^{2}}{4a^{-1}b^{3}}$ and express your answer with positive indices only. (3 marks)
(b) Hence find the value of the expression when $a=2$ and $b=1$. (1 mark)
math_p1_01.markingSchemeEn:
(a) Expand the numerator first: $(2a^{3}b^{-2})^{2}=4a^{6}b^{-4}$ …… 1 mark
    Cancel the coefficients and apply $\dfrac{a^{m}}{a^{n}}=a^{m-n}$: $\dfrac{4a^{6}b^{-4}}{4a^{-1}b^{3}}=a^{6-(-1)}b^{-4-3}=a^{7}b^{-7}$ …… 1 mark
    Express with positive indices: $\dfrac{a^{7}}{b^{7}}$ …… 1 mark
(b) Substitute $a=2,\ b=1$: $\dfrac{2^{7}}{1^{7}}=128$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_01.explanationEn: This question uses three laws of indices in succession. Two errors account for most lost marks. First, when expanding $(2a^{3}b^{-2})^{2}$, candidates forget to square the coefficient 2 as well, obtaining 2 instead of 4. Second, when dividing, they forget that subtracting a negative index adds, and write $b^{-4-3}$ as $b^{-1}$. The question states "positive indices only", so stopping at $a^{7}b^{-7}$ is not a complete answer.

math_p1_02.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(1)] (4 marks)

It is given that $S=\dfrac{a(1-r^{n})}{1-r}$, where $r\neq 1$.
(a) Express $a$ in terms of $S$, $r$ and $n$. (2 marks)
(b) If $S=62$, $r=2$ and $n=5$, find the value of $a$. (2 marks)
math_p1_02.markingSchemeEn:
(a) Multiply both sides by $(1-r)$: $S(1-r)=a(1-r^{n})$ …… 1 mark
    Divide both sides by $(1-r^{n})$: $a=\dfrac{S(1-r)}{1-r^{n}}$ …… 1 mark
(b) Substitute: $1-r=1-2=-1$ and $1-r^{n}=1-2^{5}=-31$ …… 1 mark
    $a=\dfrac{62\times(-1)}{-31}=2$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_02.explanationEn: The general rule for changing the subject of a formula: isolate the whole term containing the required variable first, then divide away the factors attached to it. Here two negative signs divide to give a positive, which is the commonest careless slip. It is far safer to evaluate $1-r$ and $1-r^{n}$ separately as numbers before substituting than to substitute into the whole expression at once.

math_p1_03.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(1)] (5 marks)

(a) Factorize $4x^{2}-9y^{2}$. (1 mark)
(b) Hence factorize $4x^{2}-9y^{2}-2x-3y$. (4 marks)
math_p1_03.markingSchemeEn:
(a) Difference of two squares: $4x^{2}-9y^{2}=(2x)^{2}-(3y)^{2}=(2x-3y)(2x+3y)$ …… 1 mark
(b) Observe the last two terms: $-2x-3y=-(2x+3y)$ …… 1 mark
    Substitute the result of (a): $(2x-3y)(2x+3y)-(2x+3y)$ …… 1 mark
    Take out the common factor $(2x+3y)$ …… 1 mark
    $=(2x+3y)(2x-3y-1)$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_03.explanationEn: The word "hence" is a binding instruction: part (b) must use the result of (a), and starting afresh does not meet the requirement even if the answer is correct. The key step is seeing that $-2x-3y$ is exactly $-(2x+3y)$, that is, the last two terms contain one of the factors from (a). Whenever a question reads "factorize A; hence factorize B", the first move is always to look for the factors of A inside B.

math_p1_04.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(1)] (5 marks)

A shop sets the marked price of an article at $60\%$ above its cost price. The article is later sold at a $20\%$ discount on the marked price, and a profit of $\$84$ is still made.
(a) Find the cost price of the article. (3 marks)
(b) Find the percentage profit of the sale, based on the cost price. (2 marks)
math_p1_04.markingSchemeEn:
(a) Let the cost price be $\$C$. Marked price $=1.6C$ …… 1 mark
    Selling price $=0.8\times 1.6C=1.28C$, so profit $=1.28C-C=0.28C$ …… 1 mark
    $0.28C=84 \Rightarrow C=300$ …… 1 mark
(b) Percentage profit $=\dfrac{84}{300}\times100\%=28\%$ …… 2 marks
math_p1_04.explanationEn: The single thread running through this type of question is that every percentage must be pinned to the correct base. The marked price is based on the cost price ($1.6C$), the discount is based on the marked price ($0.8\times1.6C$), and the question states that the percentage profit is based on the cost price. The commonest error is to treat a $20\%$ discount as "$20\%$ off the cost price" and write $1.6C-0.2C$: the base of the discount is the marked price, not the cost price.

math_p1_05.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(1)] (6 marks)

Let $f(x)=2x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+6$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. It is given that the remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-1)$ is $-6$, and that $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x)$.
(a) Find the values of $a$ and $b$. (4 marks)
(b) Factorize $f(x)$ into a product of three linear factors. (2 marks)
math_p1_05.markingSchemeEn:
(a) By the remainder theorem, $f(1)=-6$: $2+a+b+6=-6 \Rightarrow a+b=-14$ …… 1 mark
    By the factor theorem, $f(-2)=0$: $-16+4a-2b+6=0 \Rightarrow 2a-b=5$ …… 1 mark
    Solving simultaneously: $3a=-9 \Rightarrow a=-3$ …… 1 mark
    $b=-14-(-3)=-11$ …… 1 mark
(b) $f(x)=2x^{3}-3x^{2}-11x+6$. Dividing by $(x+2)$ gives the quotient $2x^{2}-7x+3$ …… 1 mark
    $2x^{2}-7x+3=(2x-1)(x-3)$, so $f(x)=(x+2)(2x-1)(x-3)$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_05.explanationEn: The remainder theorem and the factor theorem are two statements of the same result: a factor is the case where the remainder is zero. This question uses both, each giving one equation, which are then solved simultaneously. The division of labour in (b) must be clear: the factor theorem supplies one factor only, and the quotient must be obtained by long division (or synthetic division) before that quadratic is factorized. Candidates who instead guess the remaining factors almost always fail when the leading coefficient is not 1, as it is 2 here.

math_p1_06.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(1)] (5 marks)

Each interior angle of a regular $n$-sided polygon is $132^{\circ}$ greater than each exterior angle.
(a) Find the size of each exterior angle. (2 marks)
(b) Find the value of $n$. (1 mark)
(c) Find the sum of the interior angles of the regular $n$-sided polygon. (2 marks)
math_p1_06.markingSchemeEn:
(a) Let each exterior angle be $x^{\circ}$, so each interior angle is $(x+132)^{\circ}$.
    Interior and exterior angles are supplementary: $x+(x+132)=180$ …… 1 mark
    $2x=48 \Rightarrow x=24$, so each exterior angle is $24^{\circ}$ …… 1 mark
(b) The sum of the exterior angles of a polygon is $360^{\circ}$, so $n=\dfrac{360}{24}=15$ …… 1 mark
(c) Sum of interior angles $=(n-2)\times180^{\circ}=(15-2)\times180^{\circ}$ …… 1 mark
    $=2340^{\circ}$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_06.explanationEn: This question links two properties: the interior and exterior angles at one vertex lie on a straight line and therefore sum to $180^{\circ}$, and the exterior angles of any polygon sum to $360^{\circ}$. Finding the exterior angle first and then $n$ is much quicker than starting from the interior angle, because the exterior angles have a fixed sum while the interior angles require $(n-2)\times180$ to be solved backwards. This order, exterior angle first and $n$ second, is worth remembering.

math_p1_07.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(1)] (6 marks)

The marks of 12 students in a class in a test are as follows:

$32,\ 35,\ 35,\ 38,\ 41,\ 43,\ 47,\ 47,\ 47,\ 52,\ 55,\ 58$

(a) Find the median of the data. (2 marks)
(b) Find the mode and the range of the data. (2 marks)
(c) Find the inter-quartile range of the data. (2 marks)
math_p1_07.markingSchemeEn:
(a) The data are already in order and there are 12 values, so the median is the mean of the 6th and 7th values …… 1 mark
    $\dfrac{43+47}{2}=45$ …… 1 mark
(b) The value occurring most often is $47$ (three times), so the mode is $47$ …… 1 mark
    Range $=58-32=26$ …… 1 mark
(c) The lower quartile $Q_{1}$ is the median of the first 6 values $=\dfrac{35+38}{2}=36.5$ …… 1 mark
    The upper quartile $Q_{3}$ is the median of the last 6 values $=\dfrac{47+52}{2}=49.5$
    Inter-quartile range $=49.5-36.5=13$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_07.explanationEn: The three measures have different natures and must be kept distinct in an answer: the median and the quartiles are about position, the mode is about frequency, and the range and inter-quartile range measure dispersion. The number of values here is even, so the median must be the mean of the two middle values; the same applies to the quartiles, where the data are split into halves and the median of each half is taken. Candidates commonly include the median 45 in one of the halves, which makes both $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{3}$ wrong.

math_p1_08.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(2)] (5 marks)

Two similar cones have heights in the ratio $2:3$.
(a) If the volume of the smaller cone is $40\text{ cm}^{3}$, find the volume of the larger cone. (3 marks)
(b) If the total surface area of the larger cone is $90\text{ cm}^{2}$, find the total surface area of the smaller cone. (2 marks)
math_p1_08.markingSchemeEn:
(a) For similar solids the ratio of volumes is the cube of the ratio of lengths: $V_{1}:V_{2}=2^{3}:3^{3}=8:27$ …… 1 mark
    $\dfrac{40}{V_{2}}=\dfrac{8}{27}$ …… 1 mark
    $V_{2}=40\times\dfrac{27}{8}=135\text{ cm}^{3}$ …… 1 mark
(b) For similar solids the ratio of areas is the square of the ratio of lengths: $A_{1}:A_{2}=2^{2}:3^{2}=4:9$ …… 1 mark
    $A_{1}=90\times\dfrac{4}{9}=40\text{ cm}^{2}$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_08.explanationEn: Similar solids involve only three ratios: length $k$, area $k^{2}$ and volume $k^{3}$. Part (a) deliberately goes from small to large and part (b) from large to small, to test whether candidates notice the direction of multiplication and division. If both parts are computed in the same direction, one of them must be wrong. Writing down the direction of the ratio first, that is, which quantity is the 2 and which the 3, before substituting numbers, prevents most of the marks lost here.

math_p1_09.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(2)] (7 marks)

In $\triangle ABC$, $AB=8\text{ cm}$, $AC=5\text{ cm}$ and $\angle BAC=60^{\circ}$.
(a) Find $BC$. (3 marks)
(b) Find the area of $\triangle ABC$, giving your answer in surd form. (2 marks)
(c) Find the distance from $A$ to $BC$, correct to 3 significant figures. (2 marks)
math_p1_09.markingSchemeEn:
(a) By the cosine formula: $BC^{2}=AB^{2}+AC^{2}-2(AB)(AC)\cos\angle BAC$ …… 1 mark
    $=8^{2}+5^{2}-2(8)(5)\cos 60^{\circ}=64+25-40=49$ …… 1 mark
    $BC=7\text{ cm}$ …… 1 mark
(b) Area $=\dfrac{1}{2}(AB)(AC)\sin\angle BAC=\dfrac{1}{2}(8)(5)\sin 60^{\circ}$ …… 1 mark
    $=20\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=10\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^{2}$ …… 1 mark
(c) Let the required distance be $h$. Taking $BC$ as the base: $\dfrac{1}{2}(7)h=10\sqrt{3}$ …… 1 mark
    $h=\dfrac{20\sqrt{3}}{7}\approx 4.95\text{ cm}$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_09.explanationEn: Part (c) is the designed point of this question: to find the distance from a point to a line there is no need to construct a perpendicular and solve another triangle, because the area of one triangle can be expressed using two different bases and heights, so the result of (b) becomes the equation for (c) directly. This use of area as a bridge appears very often in Paper 1 and is worth making a habit. Note also that (b) asks for surd form while (c) asks for 3 significant figures: keeping the surd through the working and approximating only at the last step avoids accumulated rounding error.

math_p1_10.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(2)] (7 marks)

The first term of an arithmetic sequence is $5$ and the common difference is $4$.
(a) Find the 20th term of the sequence. (2 marks)
(b) Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the sequence. (2 marks)
(c) Find the least positive integer $n$ such that the sum of the first $n$ terms exceeds $1000$. (3 marks)
math_p1_10.explanationEn: Part (c) is the familiar "find the least $n$" type in Paper 1. The quadratic inequality may be solved, or values may be tried as above; but whichever method is used, both $n=21$ failing and $n=22$ succeeding must be shown. Writing $n=22$ without testing $n=21$ does not establish that it is the least value, and step marks are deducted. The same applies to questions on arithmetic and geometric sequences and on compound interest.

math_p1_11.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(2)] (6 marks)

In circle $O$, $AB$ is a diameter and $C$ is another point on the circle with $\angle CAB=34^{\circ}$. $TC$ is the tangent to the circle at $C$, and $T$ and $B$ lie on opposite sides of the line $AC$.
(a) Find $\angle ACB$, giving a reason. (2 marks)
(b) Find $\angle ABC$. (2 marks)
(c) Find $\angle TCA$, giving a reason. (2 marks)
math_p1_11.referenceAnswerEn:
(a) $\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$ (angle in semi-circle)
(b) $\angle ABC=56^{\circ}$
(c) $\angle TCA=56^{\circ}$ (angle in alternate segment)
math_p1_11.markingSchemeEn:
(a) $AB$ is a diameter, so $\angle ACB$ is an angle in a semi-circle …… 1 mark
    Therefore $\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$ …… 1 mark
(b) Angle sum of triangle: $\angle ABC=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-34^{\circ}$ …… 1 mark
    $=56^{\circ}$ …… 1 mark
(c) The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment, so $\angle TCA=\angle ABC$ …… 1 mark
    $=56^{\circ}$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_11.explanationEn:
In circle geometry the reason carries as many marks as the answer. The three parts correspond to three properties: the angle in a semi-circle is a right angle, the angle sum of a triangle, and the tangent-chord angle. The word most easily misread in the tangent-chord property is "alternate": $\angle TCA$ corresponds to the angle in the segment on the other side of the chord $CA$, namely $\angle ABC$, and not to $\angle CAB$ on the same side. Marking the chord on the diagram first and then confirming which segment has been taken prevents this error.

[Revised 2026-08-27] The original text read "T and B lie on the same side of the line AC". In that configuration $\angle TCA=124^{\circ}$, which does not match the reference answer of $56^{\circ}$. The point being tested is that the tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment ($56^{\circ}$), so the question has been revised to "opposite sides".

math_p1_12.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(2)] (6 marks)

Five numbers are $4,\ 7,\ 9,\ 12,\ 18$.
(a) Find the mean of the five numbers. (1 mark)
(b) Find the standard deviation of the five numbers, correct to 3 significant figures. (3 marks)
(c) If $6$ is added to each of the five numbers, find the mean and the standard deviation of the new set. (2 marks)
math_p1_12.referenceAnswerEn:
(a) Mean $=10$
(b) Standard deviation $\approx 4.77$
(c) New mean $=16$; new standard deviation $\approx 4.77$ (unchanged)
math_p1_12.markingSchemeEn:
(a) $\bar{x}=\dfrac{4+7+9+12+18}{5}=\dfrac{50}{5}=10$ …… 1 mark
(b) Deviations from the mean: $-6,\ -3,\ -1,\ 2,\ 8$ …… 1 mark
    Sum of squared deviations $=36+9+1+4+64=114$ …… 1 mark
    Standard deviation $=\sqrt{\dfrac{114}{5}}=\sqrt{22.8}\approx 4.77$ …… 1 mark
(c) Adding a constant to every value adds that constant to the mean: $10+6=16$ …… 1 mark
    The deviations from the mean are unchanged, so the standard deviation is unchanged at $4.77$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_12.explanationEn: Part (c) tests a central property of measures of dispersion: the standard deviation measures the spread between the data, not the size of the data themselves. Translating the whole set leaves every gap exactly as it was, so the standard deviation does not change. Verifying this by recomputing is slow and error-prone; it should be deduced from the property directly. By contrast, multiplying all five numbers by $k$ multiplies the standard deviation by $|k|$. Unchanged under translation, proportional under scaling: those are the two rules of this topic.

math_p1_13.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(2)] (6 marks)

A bag contains $5$ red balls and $3$ blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random from the bag without replacement.
(a) Find the probability that both balls are red. (2 marks)
(b) Find the probability that one ball is red and the other is blue. (2 marks)
(c) Find the probability that at least one blue ball is drawn. (2 marks)
math_p1_13.markingSchemeEn:
(a) $P(\text{both red})=\dfrac{5}{8}\times\dfrac{4}{7}$ …… 1 mark
    $=\dfrac{20}{56}=\dfrac{5}{14}$ …… 1 mark
(b) One red and one blue can occur in two orders (red then blue, blue then red) …… 1 mark
    $P=2\times\dfrac{5}{8}\times\dfrac{3}{7}=\dfrac{30}{56}=\dfrac{15}{28}$ …… 1 mark
(c) The complementary event of "at least one blue" is "both red" …… 1 mark
    $P=1-\dfrac{5}{14}=\dfrac{9}{14}$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_13.explanationEn: Each part demonstrates one standard technique. In (a) there is no replacement, so both the numerator and the denominator fall by one on the second draw. In (b) the commonest loss of marks is omitting the factor 2: "one red and one blue" does not specify an order, and both orders must be counted. Part (c) demonstrates the complementary event: whenever the words "at least" appear, consider what the opposite is. Here the opposite is a single case (both red), which is quicker and less error-prone than listing "one blue" and "two blue" separately.

math_p1_14.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(2)] (7 marks)

It is given that $z$ varies directly as $x$ and inversely as the square of $y$. When $x=4$ and $y=3$, $z=8$.
(a) Express $z$ in terms of $x$ and $y$. (3 marks)
(b) Find the value of $z$ when $x=9$ and $y=2$. (2 marks)
(c) If $x$ is increased by $25\%$ and $y$ is decreased by $20\%$, find the percentage change in $z$, correct to 3 significant figures. (2 marks)
math_p1_14.markingSchemeEn:
(a) Let $z=\dfrac{kx}{y^{2}}$, where $k$ is a non-zero constant …… 1 mark
    Substitute $x=4,\ y=3,\ z=8$: $8=\dfrac{4k}{9}$ …… 1 mark
    $k=18$, so $z=\dfrac{18x}{y^{2}}$ …… 1 mark
(b) $z=\dfrac{18(9)}{2^{2}}=\dfrac{162}{4}$ …… 1 mark
    $=40.5$ …… 1 mark
(c) New value $z'=\dfrac{18(1.25x)}{(0.8y)^{2}}=\dfrac{1.25}{0.64}\times\dfrac{18x}{y^{2}}=1.953125\,z$ …… 1 mark
    Percentage change $=(1.953125-1)\times100\%\approx +95.3\%$ (an increase) …… 1 mark
math_p1_14.explanationEn: Part (c) separates the candidates. The correct method is to substitute the new $x$ and $y$ into the relation and let each percentage change act through its own power: $x$ appears to the first power, so multiply by $1.25$; $y$ appears squared, so divide by $0.8^{2}=0.64$ and not by $0.8$. The commonest error is to read a $20\%$ decrease in $y$ as a $20\%$ increase in $z$, ignoring the square. In any percentage-change question, writing down $(1+p)$ together with its power before calculating is safer than working mentally.

math_p1_15.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section A(2)] (7 marks)

In the rectangular coordinate plane, $A=(-1,\ 2)$ and $B=(5,\ 6)$.
(a) Find the coordinates of $M$, the mid-point of $AB$. (1 mark)
(b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. (3 marks)
(c) Find the equation of the circle with $AB$ as a diameter. (3 marks)
math_p1_15.markingSchemeEn:
(a) $M=\left(\dfrac{-1+5}{2},\ \dfrac{2+6}{2}\right)=(2,\ 4)$ …… 1 mark
(b) Slope of $AB=\dfrac{6-2}{5-(-1)}=\dfrac{4}{6}=\dfrac{2}{3}$ …… 1 mark
    Slope of the perpendicular bisector $=-\dfrac{3}{2}$ (the product of the slopes of perpendicular lines is $-1$) …… 1 mark
    Through $M(2,4)$: $y-4=-\dfrac{3}{2}(x-2)$, that is $3x+2y-14=0$ …… 1 mark
(c) The centre is $M(2,4)$; $AB=\sqrt{6^{2}+4^{2}}=\sqrt{52}$, so the radius $r=\dfrac{\sqrt{52}}{2}=\sqrt{13}$ …… 1 mark
    $(x-2)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=13$ …… 1 mark
    Expanding: $x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-8y+7=0$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_15.explanationEn: There is one easy slip in (c): $AB$ is the diameter and not the radius, so $r=\dfrac{AB}{2}$ and $r^{2}=\dfrac{52}{4}=13$. Candidates frequently take $AB^{2}=52$ as $r^{2}$, which makes the circle twice the size it should be. A safe alternative is the diameter form $(x-x_{1})(x-x_{2})+(y-y_{1})(y-y_{2})=0$: substituting $A$ and $B$ gives the same equation and serves as a check.

math_p1_16.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section B] (8 marks)

Let $f(x)=x^{2}-2kx+(k^{2}+k-6)$, where $k$ is a real number.
(a) Express the minimum value of $f(x)$ in terms of $k$. (3 marks)
(b) If the equation $f(x)=0$ has two distinct real roots, find the range of values of $k$. (3 marks)
(c) If the minimum value of $f(x)$ is $-2$, find the value of $k$. (2 marks)
math_p1_16.markingSchemeEn:
(a) Complete the square: $f(x)=x^{2}-2kx+k^{2}+(k-6)$ …… 1 mark
    $=(x-k)^{2}+(k-6)$ …… 1 mark
    Since $(x-k)^{2}\geq 0$, the minimum value is $k-6$, attained at $x=k$ …… 1 mark
(b) Discriminant $\Delta=(-2k)^{2}-4(1)(k^{2}+k-6)$ …… 1 mark
    $=4k^{2}-4k^{2}-4k+24=-4k+24$ …… 1 mark
    Two distinct real roots require $\Delta>0$: $-4k+24>0 \Rightarrow k<6$ …… 1 mark
(c) From (a): $k-6=-2$ …… 1 mark
    $k=4$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_16.explanationEn: Parts (a) and (b) look like two different routes but point to the same fact: for a parabola opening upwards, "two distinct real roots" is equivalent to "the minimum value is less than zero". From (a) the minimum is $k-6$, and $k-6<0$ gives $k<6$, exactly as the discriminant does in (b). Checking (b) against the result of (a) is a self-check that costs nothing. Note also that when completing the square the term $k^{2}$ is already present in the expression, so nothing needs to be added and subtracted; that is why the constant term was written as $k^{2}+k-6$.

math_p1_17.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section B] (8 marks)

(a) Solve the equation $\log_{3}x+\log_{3}(x-2)=1$. (4 marks)
(b) Solve the equation $2^{2x}-5(2^{x})+4=0$. (4 marks)
math_p1_17.markingSchemeEn:
(a) Combine the logarithms: $\log_{3}[x(x-2)]=1$ …… 1 mark
    Convert to index form: $x(x-2)=3^{1}=3$ …… 1 mark
    $x^{2}-2x-3=0 \Rightarrow (x-3)(x+1)=0$, giving $x=3$ or $x=-1$ …… 1 mark
    Check: $\log_{3}(-1)$ is undefined when $x=-1$, so it must be rejected. Hence $x=3$ …… 1 mark
(b) Note that $2^{2x}=(2^{x})^{2}$. Let $u=2^{x}$, where $u>0$ …… 1 mark
    The equation becomes $u^{2}-5u+4=0$ …… 1 mark
    $(u-1)(u-4)=0$, giving $u=1$ or $u=4$ …… 1 mark
    $2^{x}=1 \Rightarrow x=0$; $2^{x}=4 \Rightarrow x=2$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_17.explanationEn: Each part has one step that must be performed. In (a) the roots must be checked: combining logarithms widens the domain, so not every root obtained is admissible. Here $x=-1$ makes $\log_{3}x$ undefined and must be rejected with the reason stated; writing $x=3$ alone, without saying why the other root was discarded, loses step marks. In (b) the entry point is seeing that $2^{2x}=(2^{x})^{2}$, which allows the substitution; the condition $u>0$ should also be stated, since an exponential is always positive. Both roots happen to be positive here, but if the coefficients were changed so that a negative root appeared, that condition would be what rejects it.

math_p1_18.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section B] (8 marks)

The first term of a geometric sequence is $3$ and the common ratio is $2$.
(a) Find the 8th term of the sequence. (2 marks)
(b) Find $S_{n}$, the sum of the first $n$ terms, in terms of $n$. (3 marks)
(c) Find the least positive integer $n$ such that $S_{n}>5000$. (3 marks)
math_p1_18.explanationEn: Part (c) belongs to the same "least $n$" family as question 10, and again both ends must be verified: $n=10$ fails and $n=11$ succeeds. The difference is that $S_{n}$ for a geometric sequence contains $2^{n}$ and grows very fast, so trying values narrows the answer in one or two steps and is quicker and more reliable than taking logarithms. If logarithms are used, both sides must be taken to the same base with the inequality unchanged in direction (the base exceeds 1), and the answer must still be rounded to an integer and substituted back to verify.

math_p1_19.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section B] (7 marks)

In a cuboid $ABCDEFGH$, the base $ABCD$ is a rectangle with $AB=12\text{ cm}$ and $BC=5\text{ cm}$, and the height is $8\text{ cm}$ ($E$, $F$, $G$ and $H$ are vertically above $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ respectively).
(a) Find the length of the diagonal $AC$. (2 marks)
(b) Find the length of the space diagonal $AG$, correct to 3 significant figures. (2 marks)
(c) Find the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$, correct to 3 significant figures. (3 marks)
math_p1_19.markingSchemeEn:
(a) In $\triangle ABC$ (where $\angle ABC=90^{\circ}$): $AC=\sqrt{12^{2}+5^{2}}$ …… 1 mark
    $=\sqrt{169}=13\text{ cm}$ …… 1 mark
(b) $CG$ is perpendicular to the base, so $\angle ACG=90^{\circ}$: $AG=\sqrt{AC^{2}+CG^{2}}=\sqrt{13^{2}+8^{2}}$ …… 1 mark
    $=\sqrt{233}\approx 15.3\text{ cm}$ …… 1 mark
(c) $AC$ is the projection of $AG$ on the base, so the required angle is $\angle GAC$ …… 1 mark
    $\tan\angle GAC=\dfrac{CG}{AC}=\dfrac{8}{13}$ …… 1 mark
    $\angle GAC\approx 31.6^{\circ}$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_19.explanationEn: The whole technique of three-dimensional trigonometry is to reduce a solid problem to two successive plane right-angled triangles. Here Pythagoras' theorem is applied once in the base to find $AC$, and a second time in the vertical plane $ACG$ to find $AG$. The key to (c) is the definition of the angle between a line and a plane: it is the angle between the line and its projection on that plane. The projection of $AG$ on the base is $AC$, so the angle is $\angle GAC$ and not $\angle GAB$ or $\angle AGC$. Drawing the projection on the diagram before answering prevents the wrong angle being taken.

math_p1_20.questionEn:
[Paper 1 · Section B] (8 marks)

A group of $4$ people is to be chosen from $4$ boys and $5$ girls.
(a) Find the number of possible selections. (2 marks)
(b) Find the number of selections consisting of exactly $2$ boys and $2$ girls. (3 marks)
(c) If the group is chosen at random, find the probability that it contains at least $1$ boy. (3 marks)
math_p1_20.markingSchemeEn:
(a) Choosing $4$ from $9$ people without regard to order: $C^{9}_{4}$ …… 1 mark
    $=\dfrac{9!}{4!\,5!}=126$ …… 1 mark
(b) Boys: $C^{4}_{2}=6$ …… 1 mark
    Girls: $C^{5}_{2}=10$ …… 1 mark
    By the multiplication principle: $6\times10=60$ …… 1 mark
(c) The complementary event of "at least 1 boy" is "all girls" …… 1 mark
    Selections of all girls: $C^{5}_{4}=5$, so $P(\text{all girls})=\dfrac{5}{126}$ …… 1 mark
    $P(\text{at least 1 boy})=1-\dfrac{5}{126}=\dfrac{121}{126}$ …… 1 mark
math_p1_20.explanationEn: This question demonstrates three judgements that must be kept distinct in problems on combinations. First, whether order matters: forming a group does not involve order, so combinations are used rather than permutations. Second, two independent choices must be multiplied and not added: in (b) the boys and the girls are chosen separately, so the two counts are multiplied. Third, (c) again demonstrates the complementary event: computing "1 boy", "2 boys", "3 boys" and "4 boys" directly requires four combinations to be found and added, whereas the complement is a single case, an enormous difference in work. Whenever "at least" appears, first check whether its opposite consists of only one or two cases.
